## AGT001

**Self-hosted agent pool shared across trust boundaries**: High, Agents

**Why it matters.** Self-hosted agents keep files, caches and credentials between jobs. A pool used by projects of different trust levels lets a pipeline in a low-trust project tamper with the agent and then read or alter what a high-trust project builds or deploys.

**How to fix.** Give each trust group its own agent pool (or use ephemeral agents, e.g. scale-set agents with "tear down after each use"), and remove the pool from the projects of the other groups in Project settings > Agent pools.

**Data.** AgentQueues (`{project}/_apis/distributedtask/queues`)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `trustGroups` = `@{}`

## AGT002

**Self-hosted agent below minimum version**: Medium, Agents

**Why it matters.** Only the current major version of the agent receives security patches: Microsoft states that only 5.x agents get patches and that no new 4.x versions are published (Microsoft Learn, "Agent software version 5", 2026). Older agents also run on runtimes that no longer get fixes and can be refused by newer tasks.

**How to fix.** Check that the host operating system is supported by .NET 10 (required by agent 5.x), upgrade the OS if needed, then update the agent from the pool page (Agent pools > the pool > Update all agents). Lower minimumVersion in the config only for hosts that cannot be upgraded yet.

**Data.** AgentPools (`_apis/distributedtask/pools` + agents of self-hosted pools)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `minimumVersion` = `5.0.0`

## AGT003

**Self-hosted agent offline for a long time**: Low, Agents

**Why it matters.** An agent offline for weeks is usually a decommissioned machine still registered: it keeps its access token, clutters capacity planning and may come back unpatched.

**How to fix.** Confirm the machine is gone, then remove the agent from the pool (Agent pools > the pool > Agents > Delete). If it is still needed, bring it back online and patch it first.

**Data.** AgentPools (`_apis/distributedtask/pools` + agents of self-hosted pools)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `days` = `30`

## CST001

**Paid license assigned to an inactive user**: Medium, Cost

**Why it matters.** Basic and Basic + Test Plans licenses are billed monthly whether or not the user signs in; inactive accounts are also an access risk (leavers, forgotten guests).

**How to fix.** Confirm the user no longer needs access, then change the access level to Stakeholder (free) or remove the user in Organization settings > Users. Prefer group rules so licenses follow team membership.

**Data.** UserEntitlements (`vsaex: _apis/userentitlements`)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `days` = `90`
- `licenseTypes` = `@('express', 'advanced')`

## HYG001

**Pipeline not run recently**: Low, Hygiene

**Why it matters.** Pipelines nobody runs still hold permissions on service connections, agent pools and repositories, clutter the catalog and hide which automation is actually in use.

**How to fix.** Confirm with the owner, then delete the pipeline or disable it (Settings > Disabled). Keep the YAML in the repository history if it may be needed again.

**Data.** BuildDefinitions (`{project}/_apis/build/definitions?includeLatestBuilds&includeAllProperties`)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `days` = `90`

## HYG002

**Repository without recent commits**: Low, Hygiene

**Why it matters.** Abandoned repositories keep their permissions, service hooks and pipeline triggers, still show up in code search and audits, and nobody patches their dependencies.

**How to fix.** Confirm with the owner, then disable the repository (Repositories > the repository > Settings > Disable repository) to make it read-only, or delete it if it is no longer needed.

**Data.** RepositoryActivity (`{project}/_apis/git/repositories/{id}/commits` (latest commit))

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `days` = `180`

## IAM001

**Too many Project Collection Administrators**: High, Identity

**Why it matters.** Project Collection Administrators can change every project, pipeline, service connection, policy and permission in the organization. Each extra member is one more account whose compromise exposes everything, and broad membership makes it hard to tell who approved what.

**How to fix.** Keep only a few named owners in Project Collection Administrators. Give others the narrower role they need (Project Administrators, Build Administrators, Endpoint Administrators), and prefer an Entra ID group with access reviews over individual accounts.

**Data.** AdminGroups (`vssps: _apis/graph/groups`, `graph/users`, `graph/Memberships` (admin groups, nested groups expanded))

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `maxMembers` = `5`

## IAM002

**Inactive administrator**: High, Identity

**Why it matters.** An administrator account nobody uses keeps full rights: it typically belongs to someone who changed role or left, is rarely monitored, and is a prime target because a takeover goes unnoticed.

**How to fix.** Confirm with the owner and remove the account from the administrator groups (or from the organization). Use time-bound elevation, for example Entra ID Privileged Identity Management on the group, instead of standing admin rights.

**Data.** AdminGroups (`vssps: _apis/graph/groups`, `graph/users`, `graph/Memberships` (admin groups, nested groups expanded)); UserEntitlements (`vsaex: _apis/userentitlements`)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `days` = `90`

## IAM003

**Guest account with administrator rights**: High, Identity

**Why it matters.** A guest (Entra ID B2B) account is managed by another organization: its password, MFA and offboarding are outside your control. With administrator rights, a compromise or a missed offboarding on their side gives full control of your Azure DevOps.

**How to fix.** Remove guest accounts from administrator groups. If an external partner needs elevated access, grant the narrowest project role, time-bound, and review it regularly; consider disabling "External guest access" in Organization settings > Policies.

**Data.** AdminGroups (`vssps: _apis/graph/groups`, `graph/users`, `graph/Memberships` (admin groups, nested groups expanded))

## IAM004

**Too many Project Administrators**: Medium, Identity

**Why it matters.** Project Administrators can change pipelines, repositories, branch policies, service connections and permissions of the project, including removing the controls other checks rely on. Broad membership widens the attack surface and blurs accountability.

**How to fix.** Reduce Project Administrators to the project owners. Grant contributors the narrower groups they need (Contributors, Build Administrators, Release Administrators), ideally through Entra ID groups with periodic access reviews.

**Data.** AdminGroups (`vssps: _apis/graph/groups`, `graph/users`, `graph/Memberships` (admin groups, nested groups expanded))

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `maxMembers` = `5`

## IAM005

**Organization not connected to Microsoft Entra ID**: Medium, Identity

**Why it matters.** Administrators sign in with personal Microsoft accounts, which exist only in organizations not connected to Entra ID. Then MFA, conditional access, sign-in risk policies and central offboarding cannot be enforced: each account is protected only by its owner's own settings.

**How to fix.** Connect the organization to your Microsoft Entra ID tenant (Organization settings > Microsoft Entra), map existing users to work accounts, then enforce MFA and conditional access in Entra ID.

**Data.** AdminGroups (`vssps: _apis/graph/groups`, `graph/users`, `graph/Memberships` (admin groups, nested groups expanded))

## PIP001

**Production environment without approvals or checks**: High, Pipelines

**Why it matters.** Without checks on the environment, any pipeline that can target it deploys straight to production: no approval, no branch control, no required template. A mistaken or malicious change reaches users unreviewed.

**How to fix.** In Pipelines > Environments > the environment > Approvals and checks, add an Approval and Branch control (only the default branch); consider Required template so deployments go through the approved pipeline template.

**Data.** Environments (`{project}/_apis/distributedtask/environments` + check configurations)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `productionPatterns` = `@('prod', 'prod-*', 'prod_*', '*-prod', '*_prod', '*-prod-*', '*production*', '*produzione*', 'prd', 'prd-*', '*-prd', 'live')`

## PIP002

**Production environment without Required template check**: Medium, Pipelines

**Why it matters.** Approvals check who deploys, not how. Without a Required template check, a pipeline can deploy to production with arbitrary steps, skipping the security scans, tests and controls built into the approved template.

**How to fix.** In Pipelines > Environments > the environment > Approvals and checks, add "Required template" pointing to your approved pipeline template, so only pipelines that extend it can deploy.

**Data.** Environments (`{project}/_apis/distributedtask/environments` + check configurations)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `productionPatterns` = `@('prod', 'prod-*', 'prod_*', '*-prod', '*_prod', '*-prod-*', '*production*', '*produzione*', 'prd', 'prd-*', '*-prd', 'live')`

## PIP003

**Classic (non-YAML) build pipeline**: Low, Pipelines

**Why it matters.** Classic pipelines are not versioned with the code, cannot be reviewed in pull requests, cannot extend required templates and receive no new features.

**How to fix.** Export the pipeline to YAML (pipeline editor > Export to YAML), commit it, create a YAML pipeline from it and delete the classic one. Then disable classic pipeline creation in Organization settings.

**Data.** BuildDefinitions (`{project}/_apis/build/definitions?includeLatestBuilds&includeAllProperties`)

## PIP004

**Production stage of a classic release without approval**: High, Pipelines

**Why it matters.** A classic release stage with only automatic approval and no gates deploys to production as soon as a release is created or the previous stage succeeds. A mistaken or malicious build reaches users without anyone reviewing it.

**How to fix.** In the release pipeline, open the pre-deployment conditions of the stage and add at least one manual approver (a group, not one person), and consider gates such as Azure Monitor alerts. Better: move the release to a YAML pipeline that deploys to an environment with approvals and checks.

**Data.** ReleaseDefinitions (`vsrm: {project}/_apis/release/definitions` + each definition (variable values discarded))

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `productionPatterns` = `@('prod', 'prod-*', 'prod_*', '*-prod', '*_prod', '*-prod-*', '*production*', '*produzione*', 'prd', 'prd-*', '*-prd', 'live')`

## PIP005

**Release creator can approve their own production deployment**: Medium, Pipelines

**Why it matters.** When the person who creates a release may also approve it, one account is enough to push a change to production: the approval becomes a formality and separation of duties is lost.

**How to fix.** In the pre-deployment conditions of the stage, open Approval policies and enable "The user requesting a release or deployment should not approve it". Use an approver group with at least two members.

**Data.** ReleaseDefinitions (`vsrm: {project}/_apis/release/definitions` + each definition (variable values discarded))

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `productionPatterns` = `@('prod', 'prod-*', 'prod_*', '*-prod', '*_prod', '*-prod-*', '*production*', '*produzione*', 'prd', 'prd-*', '*-prd', 'live')`

## REL001

**Pipeline fails too often**: Medium, Reliability

**Why it matters.** A pipeline that fails often trains people to ignore red builds and re-run until green, so real defects and security gate failures slip through; it also wastes agent time and delays delivery.

**How to fix.** Open the recent failed runs, separate flaky tests and infrastructure errors from real defects, fix or quarantine the flaky parts, and track the failure rate until it is below the threshold.

**Data.** Builds (`{project}/_apis/build/builds?maxBuildsPerDefinition=50`)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `maxFailureRate` = `0.3`
- `minimumRuns` = `5`
- `runs` = `20`

## SEC001

**Service connection authorized for all pipelines**: High, Security

**Why it matters.** Any pipeline in the project, including one created tomorrow from a feature branch, can use the credential without an approval, so anyone who can edit a pipeline can act with its permissions.

**How to fix.** In Project settings > Service connections > Security, disable "Grant access permission to all pipelines" and authorize only the pipelines that need it. Add approvals and checks for production connections.

**Data.** ServiceConnections (`{project}/_apis/serviceendpoint/endpoints` + pipeline permissions)

## SEC002

**Azure service connection uses a client secret**: High, Security

**Why it matters.** A client secret is a long-lived credential: it expires and breaks deployments, and if leaked it works from anywhere until revoked. Workload identity federation issues short-lived tokens and stores no secret.

**How to fix.** Convert the service connection to workload identity federation (Edit > Convert in the service connection page), or recreate it with that scheme, then delete the old client secret in Entra ID.

**Data.** ServiceConnections (`{project}/_apis/serviceendpoint/endpoints` + pipeline permissions)

## SEC003

**Default branch without required reviewers**: Medium, Security

**Why it matters.** Without a blocking minimum-reviewers policy, anyone with contribute rights can push or merge to the default branch, and pipelines deploy whatever lands there. One compromised account is enough to ship code.

**How to fix.** In Project settings > Repositories > Policies (or the branch policies of the default branch), enable "Require a minimum number of reviewers" as a required policy, with at least the configured number of reviewers and without allowing requestors to approve their own changes.

**Data.** Repositories (`{project}/_apis/git/repositories`); Policies (`{project}/_apis/policy/configurations`)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `allowSelfApproval` = `False`
- `minimumApprovers` = `1`

## SEC004

**Public project**: Medium, Security

**Why it matters.** Anyone on the internet can read the code, work items, pipeline logs and artifacts of a public project. Logs and build outputs often leak internal hostnames, configuration and occasionally secrets.

**How to fix.** If the project is not meant to be open source, set Project settings > Overview > Visibility to Private. If it is, review pipeline logs and artifacts for internal data and disable "Allow public projects" at organization level for everything else.

**Data.** Projects (`_apis/projects`)

## SEC005

**Pipeline security settings disabled**: High, Security

**Why it matters.** These settings limit what a pipeline job token can reach and what a queue-time user can inject. With them off, one compromised pipeline can read or change repositories and resources across the organization.

**How to fix.** Enable the listed settings in Organization settings > Pipelines > Settings (enforced for every project) or, if not enforced there, in Project settings > Pipelines > Settings.

**Data.** BuildGeneralSettings (`{project}/_apis/build/generalsettings`)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `required` = `@('enforceJobAuthScope', 'enforceReferencedRepoScopedToken', 'enforceSettableVar', 'enableShellTasksArgsSanitizing')`

## SEC006

**Pull requests from forks get secrets or a full-access token**: High, Security

**Why it matters.** Anyone can open a pull request from a fork. If those builds receive pipeline secrets or a job token with full access, the author of the pull request can change the pipeline to print the secrets or act on the organization.

**How to fix.** In the pipeline triggers, turn off "Make secrets available to builds of forks" and "Make fork builds have the same permissions as regular builds". Better: in Organization/Project settings > Pipelines > Settings, limit building pull requests from forked GitHub repositories to "Securely build" or disable it.

**Data.** BuildDefinitions (`{project}/_apis/build/definitions?includeLatestBuilds&includeAllProperties`); BuildGeneralSettings (`{project}/_apis/build/generalsettings`)

## SEC007

**Azure service connection uses a certificate**: Medium, Security

**Why it matters.** A certificate is stronger than a client secret but is still a long-lived credential stored in Azure DevOps that must be rotated. Workload identity federation stores no credential at all.

**How to fix.** Convert the service connection to workload identity federation, then remove the certificate from the app registration in Entra ID.

**Data.** ServiceConnections (`{project}/_apis/serviceendpoint/endpoints` + pipeline permissions)

## SEC008

**Variable group with secrets authorized for all pipelines**: High, Security

**Why it matters.** Every pipeline in the project, including one created from a feature branch, can read the secrets of this variable group without approval. Anyone who can edit a pipeline can print or exfiltrate them.

**How to fix.** In Pipelines > Library > the variable group > Pipeline permissions, remove "open access" and authorize only the pipelines that need it. Add approvals for production secrets, or link the group to Azure Key Vault with restricted access.

**Data.** VariableGroups (`{project}/_apis/distributedtask/variablegroups` + pipeline permissions (values discarded))

## SEC009

**Credential stored as a plain-text variable in a variable group**: Critical, Security

**Why it matters.** A variable not marked as secret is shown in clear text in the UI, returned by the REST API to anyone who can read the variable group, and printed unmasked in pipeline logs. A credential stored this way must be considered leaked.

**How to fix.** Revoke and rotate the credential now. Store the new one as a secret variable (lock icon) or, better, in Azure Key Vault linked to the variable group; prefer workload identity federation where the target supports it.

**Data.** VariableGroups (`{project}/_apis/distributedtask/variablegroups` + pipeline permissions (values discarded))

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `nameExclusions` = `@('*url', '*uri', '*endpoint', '*id', '*name', '*path', '*type', '*scope', '*expiry', '*expiration', '*length', '*header', '*audience', '*issuer')`
- `namePatterns` = `@('*pat', '*pat_*', '*password*', '*passwd*', '*pwd*', '*secret*', '*token*', '*apikey*', '*api_key*', '*connectionstring*', '*privatekey*')`

## SEC010

**Secure file authorized for all pipelines**: High, Security

**Why it matters.** Secure files hold signing certificates, provisioning profiles and keys. Open to every pipeline, any pipeline author can download them and sign or publish as the organization.

**How to fix.** In Pipelines > Library > Secure files > the file > Pipeline permissions, remove open access and authorize only the pipelines that need it; add an approval check for signing material.

**Data.** SecureFiles (`{project}/_apis/distributedtask/securefiles` + pipeline permissions)

## SEC011

**Credential stored as a plain-text variable in a pipeline definition**: Critical, Security

**Why it matters.** A pipeline variable not marked as secret is visible in the pipeline editor, returned by the REST API to anyone who can read the pipeline, and printed unmasked in logs. A credential stored this way must be considered leaked.

**How to fix.** Revoke and rotate the credential now. Store the new one as a secret pipeline variable (lock icon), in a variable group linked to Azure Key Vault, or replace it with a service connection using workload identity federation.

**Data.** BuildDefinitions (`{project}/_apis/build/definitions?includeLatestBuilds&includeAllProperties`)

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `nameExclusions` = `@('*url', '*uri', '*endpoint', '*id', '*name', '*path', '*type', '*scope', '*expiry', '*expiration', '*length', '*header', '*audience', '*issuer')`
- `namePatterns` = `@('*pat', '*pat_*', '*password*', '*passwd*', '*pwd*', '*secret*', '*token*', '*apikey*', '*api_key*', '*connectionstring*', '*privatekey*')`

## SEC012

**Credential stored as a plain-text variable in a classic release**: Critical, Security

**Why it matters.** A release or stage variable not marked as secret is visible in the release editor, returned by the REST API to anyone who can read the release, and printed unmasked in deployment logs. A credential stored this way must be considered leaked.

**How to fix.** Revoke and rotate the credential now. Store the new one as a secret variable (lock icon), in a variable group linked to Azure Key Vault, or replace it with a service connection using workload identity federation.

**Data.** ReleaseDefinitions (`vsrm: {project}/_apis/release/definitions` + each definition (variable values discarded))

**Parameters** (defaults):

- `nameExclusions` = `@('*url', '*uri', '*endpoint', '*id', '*name', '*path', '*type', '*scope', '*expiry', '*expiration', '*length', '*header', '*audience', '*issuer')`
- `namePatterns` = `@('*pat', '*pat_*', '*password*', '*passwd*', '*pwd*', '*secret*', '*token*', '*apikey*', '*api_key*', '*connectionstring*', '*privatekey*')`
